title: rwst/Square-Roots
abstract: A Lean 4 / Mathlib development of a paper, which answers a problem by Dubickas. Dubickas (Glasgow Math. J. 48 (2006), 331–336) splits the reals α > 1 in two: α lies in 𝒵 when some real ξ ≠ 0 makes every integral part ⌊ξαⁿ⌋, n ≥ 1, even, and in 𝒮 otherwise. At α = 3/2 this is Mahler's question, and open; his Problem 3 asks whether √3 lies in 𝒮 or in 𝒵. This formalization settles that question and the whole square-root slice: √3 ∈ 𝒵 by an explicit ξ = 1.34160899796…, and for an integer m ≥ 2 one has √m ∈ 𝒮 exactly when m = 2. The cells √5, √6, √7, √8 put four explicit points of 𝒵 in the interval (2,3), the only interval where an answer to Dubickas's Problem 5 could live; they are formalized (SZ.exists_mem_MahlerZ_Ioo_two_three) but are not separately compared, being subsumed by the compared Theorem B. The mechanism is not Diophantine approximation but the arithmetic of Cantor sets, and rests on the triviality that √m² = m is an integer: splitting n into even and odd values turns the one orbit into two base-m orbits coupled by x + √m y = σ, and a covering induction — Utz's 1951 theorem on the distance set of the Cantor discontinuum at m = 3, proved here for every base and every modulus — solves that equation inside the restricted-digit set. The same machinery at a general modulus gives, for p ≥ 2 and non-square m ≥ 3 in either of two explicit ranges, a real ξ ≠ 0 with p ∣ ⌊ξ√mⁿ⌋ for every n ≥ 1, hence integral parts that are composite from some point on; and the greedy's branching shows the witnesses for √3 have cardinality 2^ℵ₀, so all but countably many of them are transcendental. The informal account is the companion paper doi:10.13140/RG.2.2.32215.43682. Credit divides as follows, in contributor terms rather than bibliographic ones: the mathematical discovery is the Fable-5 agent's; the formalization is the Fable-5 and Opus-5 agents'; the agents also drafted the prose of the companion paper, which the author revised; the direction and the review are the author's, who is responsible for the mathematical content. Bibliographic authorship of the paper is the author's alone — the collaboration is credited in its Acknowledgements, not in its byline, as is usual for an AI tool. There is no sorry outside the deliberate placeholders in Challenge.lean, no project-defined axiom, no native_decide, and Mathlib is the only Lake dependency of the development itself.
